title: The reformers
hook: thinkers like Jamal al-Din al-Afghani and Muhammad Abduh call for renewal and education

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zafar, the last Mughal, the poet emperor exiled across the sea. Your line was the last emperor. Today, people who refused to let an ending be the end.

Why are our lands ruled by others? A restless teacher with a sharp tongue puts that question to a crowded room in Cairo: lamplight, glasses of tea, students leaning in. Then more. What have we forgotten? What would the Qur'an say about a world of steamships and newspapers? The teacher is Jamal al-Din, called al-Afghani. One of the students listening hardest is an Egyptian named Muhammad Abduh. Neither knows yet that their conversations will shape arguments Muslims are still having. Today: the reformers.
screen: `A CROWDED ROOM IN CAIRO.` → `WHY ARE WE RULED BY OTHERS?` → `A TEACHER AND A STUDENT.`

segments.voice: Start with the teacher. Al-Afghani moved from country to country; even where he was born is debated. Wherever he went, he urged Muslims to wake up, unite, and stand against foreign rule. For a time he and Abduh published a journal together in Paris, sending its pages back to Muslim readers. Then the student. Abduh grew calmer than his teacher, and came to believe the way forward ran through schools more than politics. He worked to reform teaching, including at al-Azhar, the great mosque university of Cairo, and late in life he served as Mufti of Egypt. His central conviction: reason and revelation do not fight. Read the Qur'an with an open mind, learn the sciences, and stop treating every inherited opinion as untouchable. The reformers often quoted one line of the Qur'an. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! Allah changeth not the condition of a folk until they (first) change that which is in their hearts." Change starts inside. They also leaned on a hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud: that God will send this community, at the head of every hundred years, someone who renews its religion. Renewal, in this reading, is not a betrayal of tradition; it's part of the tradition's own promise. Not everyone agrees on what they started. Some Muslims honor them as renewers who opened the door to modern education. Others say they loosened the careful methods of the old scholars too quickly. Later movements, pulling in very different directions, have claimed them. That argument is part of their legacy. The word they kept returning to was renewal.
screen: `AL-AFGHANI: WAKE UP, UNITE.` · `ABDUH: REFORM THE SCHOOLS.` · `REASON AND REVELATION DON'T FIGHT.` · `A RENEWER, AT THE HEAD OF EVERY CENTURY.` · then, large: `CHANGE THAT WHICH IS IN THEIR HEARTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one part of your life that has gone stale: a habit kept out of routine, a prayer said without attention, a friendship you only maintain. Don't throw it out; ask what it was for in the first place, and what returning to that would look like. If you pray, hold Qur'an 13:11 in mind, that change begins in the heart; if not, let the question sit with your breathing.
The reformers. Al-Afghani and Abduh, who called Muslims to renewal through education, reason and unity. Today's word.
Your line: renewal. Going back to the start can be a way forward. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims today debate the reformers' legacy in universities, mosques and journals; some schools and movements trace their approach to Abduh's emphasis on education, while others follow older scholarly methods more closely.

chat.says: Did the reformers think renewing Islam meant leaving tradition behind?
options: No. They saw renewal as part of the tradition's own promise, a renewer every hundred years.
Yes. They told Muslims to set the Qur'an aside and follow European thinkers instead.
No. They said real change comes only from new rulers, never from the heart.
